title: How Ice Climbing Works
summary: Josh and Chuck explain ice climbing, tracing its roots in mountaineering and the invention of crampons by Oscar Eckenstein, the front-pointing fangs added by Laurent Grivel, and Yvon Chouinard's ice axe redesign. They cover ice tools and leashes, mono-point versus two-point crampons, ice screws, helmets, ideal ice conditions (near-freezing alpine ice, dinner plating, chandelier and white ice), climbing techniques (flat footing, side stepping, German front pointing, traction technique), the dangers of ice climbing and fatal accidents, dry tooling controversy, and a listener mail segment about a gifted class's band names. Opening includes tour dates announcements for Vancouver and Portland.

segments.title: Live tour announcement
segments.summary: Hosts announce upcoming live shows in Vancouver (March 29, Chan Centre) and Portland (March 30, Schnitzer Concert Hall) and point listeners to the website for tickets.

segments.title: Opening banter and episode setup
segments.summary: Hosts joke around about movies including Cliffhanger and Free Solo and introduce ice climbing as the topic, noting that rock climbing skills do not automatically transfer to ice climbing.

segments.title: Origins in mountaineering and crampons
segments.summary: Ice climbing grew out of mountaineering because high alpine snow and ice forced climbers to learn to climb ice. Oscar Eckenstein invented crampons, which changed glacier travel and made step cutting unnecessary. Early crampons were strapped on boots.

segments.title: Front-pointing fangs and the mountaineering ice axe
segments.summary: Laurent Grivel added front fangs to crampons, enabling near-vertical climbing. Yvon Chouinard, founder of Patagonia, redesigned the mountaineering axe by shortening it and curving the head, creating a distinct ice tool. The axe is used for self arrest and for pulling up on ice.

segments.title: Ice tools, leashes and mono-point vs two-point crampons
segments.summary: Discussion of ice tools, including Petzl models with ergonomic grips, the choice between leashed and unleashed tools, and the trade-offs between mono-point and two-point crampons. Heel spurs are also mentioned.

segments.title: Ice screws, helmets and gear
segments.summary: Ice screws are placed to protect climbers because ice routes lack permanent bolts. Helmets are essential due to falling ice. Overhead hazards are greater than in rock climbing. Places to climb include North America, Norway, Iceland, the Alps, Greece, Scotland, and the Ray competition site.

segments.title: Ideal ice conditions
segments.summary: Good ice is typically older alpine ice that has been near freezing for several days, appearing blue or blue-green. Very cold temperatures can cause dinner plating because ice becomes tense and brittle. White ice contains trapped air and is less solid, while chandelier ice is poor for screws. Reading the ice is a key skill.

segments.title: Climbing techniques
segments.summary: Techniques include flat footing (French technique), side stepping, the German front-pointing technique, and the traction technique using two axes. Climbing ice is physically exhausting, and free soloing ice is rare. Climbers may follow established routes on frozen waterfalls and perennial ice.

segments.title: Dangers of ice climbing and notable deaths
segments.summary: Falls in ice climbing are more dangerous than in rock climbing because falling ice accompanies the climber and tools are sharp. Sue Nott and Carrie McNeil were lost on Mount Foraker's Infinite Spur in 2006. Harry Berger died in a training accident when ice fell on him. Safety precautions include avalanche beacons and first aid kits.

segments.title: Dry tooling controversy and wrap-up
segments.summary: Dry tooling, which means using ice tools on rock, is controversial because it damages rock climbing routes. The hosts also mention a blog that mocks dangerous anchors.

segments.title: Listener mail: Gifted and talented class band names
segments.summary: A gifted and talented specialist shares band and song names created by her elementary students, with genre labels assigned by the class. The hosts praise the names.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts ask listeners to send mail and sign off with show credits.
